analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary Medicare drug discount card with catastrophic coverage for seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2003, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let Medicare beneficiaries voluntarily enroll in prescription drug card plans run by private entities such as pharmacy benefit managers and insurers, with Medicare endorsing the plans and covering the catastrophic portion of drug costs after seniors hit an annual out-of-pocket limit based on their income. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors on Medicare who lack affordable prescription drug coverage — especially low-income beneficiaries under 200% of the poverty line, who would pay no enrollment fee and face a $1,500 annual out-of-pocket cap with 10% cost-sharing above it. Private card-plan administrators (pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, and pharmacy networks) would also gain a new federally funded book of business.

how_it_helps.text: Low-income seniors (below 200% of poverty) would pay no enrollment fee and face a $1,500 annual out-of-pocket cap on covered drugs, with 10% coinsurance above that threshold.

All enrollees would get access to negotiated drug prices through an endorsed discount card, with guaranteed issuance regardless of health status and appeal rights when a needed drug is not on a plan's formulary.
Entities would be required to pass manufacturer rebates and negotiated savings on to enrolled beneficiaries, and pharmacies would have to tell buyers when a cheaper equivalent drug is available.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and Medicare's Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund would bear the cost of the catastrophic benefit and administration, and drug makers would face modest price pressure through required rebate pass-throughs; seniors would pay a $25 annual enrollment fee (waived for those below 200% of poverty).

drawbacks.text: The bill does not use Medicare's collective purchasing power to negotiate drug prices directly; instead it relies on private discount-card entities to negotiate prices with manufacturers, which would likely produce smaller and more uncertain savings for beneficiaries than direct negotiation.

The bill routes the benefit through private entities — pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, and pharmacy networks — which would receive administrative fee payments for enrolling seniors, processing claims, and administering even the catastrophic benefit, adding a private middleman layer to a public program.

Plans could use formularies with tiered cost-sharing, and beneficiaries bear cost-sharing of at least 10 percent of drug costs even after meeting their out-of-pocket limit's threshold, so coverage would still leave seniors with meaningful out-of-pocket spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the low-income seniors it targets — catastrophic drug coverage with a $1,500 out-of-pocket cap and no enrollment fee — the benefit is real and significant. But the design has serious drawbacks: it pays full negotiated prices rather than using Medicare's collective buying power to demand lower prices, it relies on private PBMs and insurers to deliver even the catastrophic benefit, and its drug-discount-card approach would likely produce modest, uneven savings for most beneficiaries. An honest supporter would acknowledge that this is a market-based alternative designed to avoid direct government negotiation, and that its savings and protections depend heavily on administrative details left to the Secretary.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2003 and never advanced — no markup, no floor vote — and the Congress ended in January 2005 without it ever coming up.

narrative.text: S. 778 was introduced in the Senate on April 3, 2003 by Senator Chuck Hagel with five Republican cosponsors.
On the day of introduction it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare legislation.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or consideration in the House, and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, no one gained from it directly; the private entities that would have won contracts as card plan administrators were not handed that new federal business, and the broader drug-benefit fight was settled instead by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003, which became law.

for.name: Sens. John Ensign, Richard Lugar, James Inhofe, and two other Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all five cosponsors were Republicans.

for.name: Senate Committee on Finance
for.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 3, 2003 and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee without action; the larger 2003 drug-benefit fight split largely along party lines, with Republicans backing private-card approaches and Democrats backing direct Medicare coverage.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) and private insurers
industries.note: The bill makes PBMs, insurers, pharmacy delivery systems, and Medicare+Choice plans the exclusive channels for the new federal drug benefit, paying them administrative fees to enroll seniors and administer even the catastrophic coverage. Medicare would not negotiate drug prices itself.

New public money for drug purchases means more customers and revenue, but the bill requires card programs to pass manufacturer rebates through to beneficiaries, pressuring prices. It does not authorize government price negotiation.

Card plans must include retail pharmacy networks with convenient access, guaranteeing the program uses neighborhood pharmacies rather than mail order alone, though plans' negotiated prices could squeeze dispensing margins.
The bill requires overhauling the standard Medigap drug benefit packages so they no longer duplicate the new federal program, pushing standalone drug coverage out of the Medigap market.
